---
title: "FABIA versus ensemble FABIA"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96, message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)
```

FABIA starts from random values, so two runs on the same data can give
different biclusters. Which ones should you trust? The **ensemble** approach
(Khamiakova, Kaiser and Shkedy, Chapter 10 of *Applied Biclustering Methods
for Big and High-Dimensional Data Using R*, Kasim et al. 2016) answers this by
running the algorithm many times and keeping only the biclusters that come back
again and again. factomics applies it to FABIA as the method `"FABIA_ENS"`.

## How the ensemble works

1. Run FABIA `runs` times, each with a different seed and, optionally, on a
   random subsample of the samples (`sample_fraction`).
2. Turn every factor of every run into a bicluster (its features and samples),
   with `fabia::extractBic()`.
3. Compute the Jaccard similarity between all biclusters: the share of
   feature-sample combinations they have in common.
4. Group the biclusters by complete-linkage hierarchical clustering, cutting
   the tree at a similarity of 0.5, so biclusters in a group share at least
   half of their elements.
5. Give each group a **reliability**: the share of runs in which it was found.
   Groups found in at least half of the runs (`min_reliability`) are robust.
6. Form the robust bicluster from the features and samples present in at
   least half of the group's biclusters (`membership`; 1 gives the core
   intersection, a small value the union "super-bicluster").

So that ensemble FABIA can be used like any other factomics method, each
robust group also becomes a factor, whose loadings and scores are the averages
over the group's members (after aligning their signs).

```{r}
library(factomics)
sim <- simulate_multiomics(n_samples = 60, seed = 1)   # 3 true factors

res <- run_factor_pipeline(sim$data, methods = c("FABIA", "FABIA_ENS"), k = 4,
                           fabia_ens_control = list(runs = 30),
                           verbose = FALSE)
res
```

We asked for 4 factors. Plain FABIA returns 4, but the ensemble keeps only the
factors it found reliably, which here are the 3 that are really in the data.

## Which biclusters are robust?

```{r, fig.height = 3}
plot_fabia_ensemble(res)
res$FABIA_ENS$meta$groups
```

Three groups were found in every run. The others turned up only in some runs:
they depend on the starting values and a single FABIA run might report one of
them as a real bicluster.

The robust biclusters themselves, with their features and samples:

```{r}
b <- res$FABIA_ENS$meta$biclusters
sapply(b, function(x) c(features = length(x$features),
                        samples = length(x$samples),
                        reliability = x$reliability))
head(b$F1$features)
```

How many of the robust features are true signal features in the simulation?

```{r}
truth <- sim$truth$feature_labels
robust <- unique(unlist(lapply(b, `[[`, "features")))
table(robust = names(truth) %in% robust, true_signal = truth)
```

Every feature in a robust bicluster is a true signal feature: the ensemble
adds no noise features.

The tree of all biclusters from all runs, as in the book (each robust group
joins at a low height):

```{r, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(res$FABIA_ENS$meta$tree, labels = FALSE, hang = -1,
     main = "Biclusters from 30 FABIA runs", xlab = "",
     sub = "Complete linkage on 1 - Jaccard")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "#E8366F")
```

## Comparing FABIA and ensemble FABIA across seeds

`factor_stability()` fits the methods once per seed and checks how much the
factors change: for every pair of seeds the factors are matched and their
loadings correlated. Since the truth is known here, it also reports how well
the true factors are recovered.

```{r}
st <- factor_stability(sim$data, methods = c("FABIA", "FABIA_ENS"), k = 4,
                       seeds = 1:5, truth = sim$truth$Z,
                       fabia_ens_control = list(runs = 30))
st
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
plot_factor_stability(st)
plot_factor_stability(st, "recovery")
```

A single FABIA run gives clearly different factors depending on the seed. The
ensemble gives practically the same factors whatever the seed, and recovers
the true factors at least as well.

## Tuning

All settings are in `fabia_ensemble_control()`, passed as
`fabia_ens_control = list(...)` in `run_factor_pipeline()`, or used directly
with the shortcut `fabia_ensemble()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fabia_ensemble(sim$data, k = 5, alpha = 0.01, cyc = 1000,
                      control = fabia_ensemble_control(
                        runs = 100,            # the book used 100 seeds
                        sample_fraction = 0.8, # also robust to the samples
                        similarity = 0.5,      # cut the tree at Jaccard 0.5
                        min_reliability = 0.5, # found in >= half the runs
                        membership = 0.5))     # majority robust bicluster
```

- More `runs` give more precise reliabilities; it costs one FABIA fit per run.
- `sample_fraction < 1` also makes the biclusters robust to which samples were
  used, a form of subsampling as described in the book.
- If no group reaches `min_reliability`, factomics stops with a message giving
  the best reliability it found; lower `min_reliability` or `similarity`.
- `alpha` (sparseness) and `k` are FABIA's own settings and are the same for
  every run.
